title: OECD Employment Outlook 2025: Can We Get Through the Demographic Crunch?
date_evidence: Search confirms 'The OECD Employment Outlook 2025 was published on July 9, 2025'; PDF path /publications/reports/2025/07/oecd-employment-outlook-2025
key_claim: The OECD Employment Outlook 2025 warns that population ageing and slower labour-force growth pose enormous challenges to living standards, making retention, participation and reskilling of existing workers central; roughly 27% of jobs across OECD countries sit in occupations at highest risk of automation.
frame_summary: Argues that demographic tightening, not just technology, makes the skills and retention of the existing workforce the binding constraint on growth, so reskilling and participation are now strategic imperatives.

title: Employment and Social Trends 2026
date_evidence: UN News 'Global employment stable but decent jobs in short supply' dated 2026/01; NextIAS coverage dated 15-01-2026; ILO flagship 'Employment and Social Trends 2026'
key_claim: The ILO projects global unemployment steady at 4.9% in 2026 but warns the broader jobs gap will reach 408 million, and that AI adoption may hit young workers seeking high-skilled roles hardest by automating the entry-threshold tasks that have been juniors' way into specialised professions.
frame_summary: Argues that headline labour-market stability masks a deteriorating jobs quality and access picture, with AI specifically threatening the entry rungs young workers use to enter skilled careers.
verbatim_quote: the broader global jobs gap - capturing people who want paid work but cannot access it - is projected to reach 408 million in 2026

title: State of the Global Workplace: 2026 Report
date_evidence: Search confirms 'The State of the Global Workplace: 2026 Report was published in April 2026, with data collected from January-December 2025'; LinkedIn Gallup post '2026 State of the Global Workplace'
key_claim: Global employee engagement fell to 20% in 2025, its lowest level since 2020, costing the world economy an estimated $10 trillion in lost productivity; manager engagement dropped to 22%, and only 12% of workers believe AI has meaningfully changed how work gets done, though global wellbeing ticked up slightly to 34% thriving for the first time in three years.
frame_summary: Argues that the workplace crisis is a management and human-connection failure, not a technology one, and that AI value depends on manager support rather than technical rollout.

title: Reskilling Revolution: Preparing 1 billion people for tomorrow's economy
date_evidence: URL path /stories/2026/01/ and page framing citing the Future of Jobs Report 2025; WEF story published January 2026
key_claim: The WEF finds 22% of jobs will be disrupted by 2030, creating 170 million new roles while displacing 92 million, and that 39% of workers' core skills are expected to change by 2030 as AI moves into workflows; only 0.5% of GDP is invested in adult lifelong learning, though more reskilling could add $6.5 trillion to GDP by 2030.
frame_summary: Argues that skills have become a binding constraint on growth and that systemic, coordinated reskilling investment is the decisive lever for the AI-era labour transition.

title: The 2026 AI Index Report, Chapter 4: Economy
date_evidence: Stanford HAI '2026 AI Index Report'; search confirms 'The 2026 report was published on April 13, 2026'
key_claim: Employment for software developers aged 22 to 25 has fallen nearly 20% from 2024, and one-third of organisations expect AI to reduce their workforce in the coming year, with anticipated reductions highest in service operations, supply chain and software engineering, even though large-scale job losses have not yet appeared in overall employment data.
frame_summary: Argues that AI's labour-market effects are showing up unevenly, concentrated in hiring pipelines and the youngest workers in exposed occupations, rather than in aggregate job losses so far.

title: The State of Organizations 2026: Three tectonic forces reshaping organizations
date_evidence: Search confirms 'the report itself was published on February 19, 2026' based on a survey conducted June to September 2025
key_claim: McKinsey finds two-thirds of leaders acknowledge their organisations are overly complex, but familiar remedies such as restructuring, delayering and downsizing are hitting diminishing returns, with the larger upside now in redesigning how work moves across the enterprise as AI is embedded.
frame_summary: Argues that another round of delayering will not fix organisational drag, and that the real gains come from redesigning workflows and integrating AI rather than from cutting more managers.

title: Challenger Report: June Layoffs Cool to 45,849, Down 53% From May; AI Leads Reasons for Fourth Consecutive Month
key_claim: US employers announced 45,849 job cuts in June, down 53% from May and 40% lower year-to-date, but AI was the leading cited reason for the fourth consecutive month at 14,029 cuts (31% of June), while technology led all sectors with 139,156 cuts this year, up 83% year on year.
frame_summary: Argues that even as the overall pace of layoffs cools, AI-driven restructuring is now the dominant named force behind job cuts, concentrated in technology.

title: Management Cuts Today Are Shaping A Leadership Shortage
key_claim: Companies are flattening management with AI, but experts warn the leadership-pipeline cost may not surface for years, as cutting the middle layer removes the roles where future leaders learn to manage, coach and coordinate.
frame_summary: Argues that AI-driven management cuts are creating a delayed but serious leadership shortage by eliminating the training ground for the next generation of leaders.

title: 5 days in the office is the least popular way to work. Bosses are mandating it anyway
date_evidence: URL path /2026/02/02/ and headline '5 days in the office is the least popular way to work. Bosses are mandating it anyway'
key_claim: More than half of the Fortune 100 now require five-day office attendance per JLL, roughly a third of all US firms require full-time in-person work, and enforcement is intensifying, with attendance tracking rising to 69% of employers and 47% of five-day firms planning to discipline or terminate non-compliant employees.
frame_summary: Argues that employers are pushing five-day mandates and enforcement despite full-time office work being the least popular arrangement with employees, widening the gap between employer power and employee preference.

title: Skill-based hiring in 2026: the 85% vs 0.14% paradox
key_claim: 85% of employers told TestGorilla they use skills-based hiring, and 53% publicly removed degree requirements (up from 30% a year earlier), yet Harvard Business School and Burning Glass Institute data show fewer than 1 in 700 (0.14%) new hires reflect it, a gap the piece argues 2026-era verifiable credentials will start to close.
frame_summary: Argues that skills-based hiring stays stuck as policy rather than practice until verifiable digital credentials give recruiters a defensible alternative to the degree, with 2026 as the inflection point.
